steps.prompt: Read both out loud. How does one comma change the meaning?
steps.reveal: A invites Grandma to dinner. B puts Grandma on the menu! Punctuation tells the reader where to pause and how to read, and sometimes it saves a life.

cards.title: Three end marks
cards.body: A full stop (.) ends a statement or a polite command. A question mark (?) ends a direct question. An exclamation mark (!) shows strong feeling, but in essays, use it rarely, and only one at a time.

cards.title: Is it really a question?
cards.telling: I wonder if it will rain?
cards.showing: I wonder if it will rain. / Will it rain?
cards.note: “I wonder if…” and “She asked whether…” tell about a question, so they end with a full stop. A real question asks the reader directly: Will it rain? Do you agree?

cards.title: Commas in a list
cards.text:
Three or more things: We packed sandwiches, apples, juice and cookies.
Actions too: We swam, ate lunch and played cards.
The last comma before “and” (the serial comma) is optional: apples, juice, and cookies.
cards.note: Pick one style and use it the whole way through. Never put a comma after the last item: “apples, juice and cookies, were packed” ✗.

cards.title: Two items? No comma
cards.body: With only two things, “and” does the job by itself: Sam and Leo, pizza or tacos. Commas start when there are three or more.

prompts: Why do you think essay writers use exclamation marks so rarely?
Do you use the serial comma (…, juice, and cookies)? Why or why not?
